analysis.one_liner: Exempts bank mergers creating companies under $10 billion from antitrust review.
analysis.headline: The House Financial Services Committee advanced the bill on a narrow 28-24 vote, but no full House vote has occurred and it sits on the Union Calendar.
analysis.plain_summary: Right now, banking regulators must reject a bank merger that would create a monopoly or substantially lessen competition. This bill says that for any deal resulting in a bank or holding company with less than $10 billion in assets, regulators may not consider those competition factors at all — they can approve the deal on other grounds regardless of what it does to competition in a market. The $10 billion figure would rise automatically each year with the growth of the U.S. economy, so it would cover more and more banks over time.
analysis.who_benefits: Banks and bank holding companies under the $10 billion line that want to merge with or acquire a rival, especially in markets where two local banks combining would leave fewer choices. Acquiring firms gain a faster, cheaper approval path because regulators can no longer block a deal on competition grounds.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Federal Deposit Insurance Act, the Bank Holding Company Act, and the Home Owners' Loan Act so that regulators 'shall not consider' whether a transaction resulting in an institution with less than $10 billion in assets would create a monopoly, substantially lessen competition, or restrain trade.

The exemption applies to acquisitions, mergers, consolidations, assumptions of liabilities, and transfers of assets by bank holding companies and savings and loan holding companies as well as banks themselves.
The $10 billion threshold is adjusted annually by the percentage increase in nominal U.S. GDP, so the carve-out grows with the economy.

analysis.who_pays: Depositors, small-business borrowers, and communities in markets where mergers would concentrate banking — fewer banks competing typically means higher fees, lower interest on savings, and less credit access, and the bill removes the legal tool regulators use to block those deals.
analysis.who_pays_short: Depositors and borrowers in concentrated markets

drawbacks.text: The exemption covers deals that could still eliminate competition in a local market — for example, a merger of the only two banks in a small town would no longer be reviewed for its effect on competition.
Because the threshold rises automatically with nominal GDP, the population of banks exempt from competition review grows every year the economy grows, without Congress ever voting to expand it.

Supporters argue sub-$10 billion banks face heavy regulatory burdens and need consolidation to stay viable, but the bill removes competition review entirely rather than streamlining it, leaving no check on the most concentrated local deals.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Easier consolidation might help some small banks absorb compliance costs, but the bill's core effect is to delete the antitrust safeguard that protects banking customers in local markets. The cost falls on depositors and borrowers in towns where choices are already thin, and the automatic GDP adjustment makes the carve-out permanent and expanding. A narrower fix — such as a streamlined review process — would address the burden without eliminating the safeguard.

outcome.mechanism: The bill cleared the House Financial Services Committee on a narrow 28-24 vote and was reported to the House in November, but it has not come up for a vote by the full House and Congress is still in session.

narrative.text: Rep. Scott Fitzgerald introduced the bill on September 10, 2025, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.
At a September 16 markup, the committee ordered the bill reported as amended by a vote of 28 to 24 — a margin narrow enough to fit within a single party's side of the committee.

The committee reported the bill with an amendment on November 4, 2025 (H. Rept. 119-365), and it was placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 317, awaiting a decision by House leadership to schedule it for a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, banks that want to merge or be acquired under the $10 billion line have gained ground: a committee controlled by the majority advanced their requested exemption past its first hurdle, and nothing in the carve-out has yet been blocked. Consumers have lost nothing yet either, since the bill has not become law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Banks seeking easier mergers, so far

sides.party_line_note: The 28-24 committee vote is narrow and consistent with a party split, but the sources do not record the party breakdown of the votes.

industries.industry: Community and mid-sized banks (under $10 billion in assets)
industries.note: The bill gives these banks and any bank acquiring into their size class a green light to consolidate without competition review, which can mean fewer local banking options, higher fees, and tighter credit for the towns they serve.

industries.industry: Bank and savings-and-loan holding companies acquiring smaller institutions
industries.note: Acquirers below the threshold get a faster, cheaper path to buying rivals because regulators are barred from weighing monopolization or competitive harm, transferring bargaining power from depositors and borrowers to consolidated owners.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits on the Union Calendar with no cosponsors and a narrow committee vote. Most bills at this stage never get floor time unless leadership decides to schedule them, so the likely path is that it stalls for the rest of the 119th Congress — though it could move as part of a broader package of financial-deregulation bills, or come up under a fast-tracked procedure if leadership chooses.
